Saving Sandfish

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A rescue mission is underway to save sandfish from extinction in the Cederberg.

Unique Selling Point:
In the remote Cederberg Mountains of South Africa, a remarkable yet little known natural spectacle takes place each year: the spawning migration of the sandfish, South Africa’s most threatened migratory freshwater fish. Every year in September, sandfish begin their ancient upstream journey in the Biedouw River – a ritual now teetering on the brink of extinction.

Once so numerous they formed waves across the river. Six years ago, fewer than 200 migratory sandfish were left in the Biedouw river. And so, Jeremy Shelton, a conservation biologist, started the Saving Sandfish project in a bid to rescue them from extinction. This is a story that goes beyond science – it’s also about cultural memory and meaning. Sarah Fransman, who grew up in a cottage on the banks of the Biedouw river, remembers how the sandfish would make a wave, “the whole school would stretch from one side to the other”. There are also paintings on cave walls in the area showing sandfish migrations on a mythic scale.



Summary:
This story will follow the urgent efforts to rescue the species from collapse. Led by the Freshwater Research Centre, a diverse team of scientists and local residents is undertaking Africa’s largest freshwater fish rescue.

Their goal is to relocate thousands of vulnerable juvenile sandfish from drying river pools – where they are vulnerable to invasive species – into cleared, alien-free farm dams where they have a fighting chance at survival.

Now, rescued sandfish that have been reared to a safe size will be released back into the wild. This will happen in the first week of September. Each is tagged with a microchip to track whether these fish return to their birthplace to spawn –the first real test of whether the intervention is working.

This is a story about the extraordinary efforts of ordinary people to restore what’s about to be lost. It’s about how we choose to respond in the face of vanishing biodiversity. The sandfish are a vital part of the Olifants-Doring River system’s ecosystem.

Script:


VO 1 In the Cederberg mountains in the Western Cape, nature thrives in abundance.

VO 2 For centuries, Spring marked the great migration of the endemic sandfish.

VO 3 Thousands headed upstream to spawn.

UPSOUND Sarah Fransman Subtitles:: When they came in the late afternoon, when the water is a bit warm, the water came alive as they made their way up. That was something beautiful. Those days are over.

VO 4 From thousands to just a few hundred - the sandfish, one of South Africa’s most threatened species, is on the brink of extinction.

UPSOUND Jeremy Shelton: They were heading for disappearance within the next decade or so unless something changed.

VO 5 And something did - a team of conservation biologists began a rescue mission unlike any other - to save the last surviving sandfish.

VO 6 Bushmans Kloof is a family owned lodge. We’re heading to one of their farm dams with general manager Gerhard Thom.

NATSOUND Govan: Am I working or am I on safari?

VO 7 It’s in this dam that the endangered freshwater migratory sandfish is getting a second chance. A sanctuary away from invasive fish species..

UPSOUND Gerhard Thom / Bushmans Kloof General Manager: We follow the San philosophy, as what the San or the hunter gatherers did in the past. By protecting and conserving wildlife and natural spaces.

VO 8 The Cederberg is famous for its rock formations, history and heritage… and thousands of rock art sites.

VO 9 It’s my first time here - and seeing rock art up close is a moving experience.

LINK: From ancient rock art to living memory, the sandfish migration has been part of this landscape for centuries. Thousands of elephants used to roam here. They’re now gone. And the sandfish could suffer the same fate.

UPSOUND Gerhard Thom / Bushman’s Kloof General Manager: It recently got discovered that the Biedouw valley is one of the last migratory places for these fish to come up and spawn and its right on our doorstep. And we knew that if we don’t step in and assist there’s a chance that this fish might go extinct.

VO 10 Known for its distinctive downturned hoover-like mouth, the sandfish from the Biedouw River graze algae off rocks which helps keep the riverbed clean. They have the smallest scales of any freshwater fish in South Africa and powerful fins used to swim great distances during their annual spawning migration.

VO 11 Jeremy Shelton is a conservation biologist at the Freshwater Research Centre who enlisted the help of Gerhard, and other farm owners in the area when they started the Saving Sandfish project six years ago. Back then, there were only 180 migratory sandfish left in the Biedouw river.

UPSOUND Jeremy Shelton / Conservation Biologist: Freshwater Research Centre: So, the Biedouw river is one of the last known spawning tributaries for the species. And once a species population drops down to below 200 in one of the last critical spawning areas, that’s a big red flag. That’s a recipe for extinction.

(Govan) How did they become endangered?

UPSOUND Jeremy Shelton / Freshwater Research Centre: Invasive species. Invasive plants that come in and infest the river banks. They suck up a lot of water, they reduce the flow and they cause a lot of erosion and sedimentation that can smother the underwater habitat but also introduced predatory fish from other parts of the world. Species like bass, blue gill that are extremely efficient predators and ja the sandfish can be displaced by an introduced predator like the bass in just a decade or so.

(Govan) Is that what happened?

UPSOUND Jeremy Shelton: That’s what happened ja

VO 12 But it wasn’t always this way. Sarah Fransman grew up in the Biedouw valley. Life was simple and quiet, so different from the bustle in the nearby town of Clanwilliam where she’s currently living with family. She plans to return home soon, to the place of the annual sandfish migration - a spectacle she vividly remembers.

UPSOUND Sarah Fransman Subtitles: The fish was food. You hit it with a small club. There was a furrow, and if they didn’t appear in the furrow, they came after. But the light on the water went like this.

(Govan) How big were they?

UPSOUND Sarah Fransman: This big.

(Govan): About half a metre?

UPSOUND Sarah Fransman: Yes!

(Govan) And how many sandfish were hung up?

UPSOUND Sarah Fransman: A bunch. These three wires were full. When they were dry, we took them we put them in a bag or a flour sack and then it went into an old cooking stove. Look, you would bite your tongue off.

VO 13 Sarah says she began to notice their decline in the nineteen nineties.

UPSOUND Sarah Fransman Subtitles: The older people have seen it. The young children don’t see it. Back then, the people were taking about it: why, what happened? But then they found out it was the black bass.

VO 14 To save them from invasive predator species, the sandfish would need to be rescued from the river as babies and moved to farm dams. And so that’s what Jeremy, a team of conservation biologists… and the community began to do.

UPSOUND Jeremy Shelton: We’ve had multiple school groups come out and help us with the sandfish rescues, members from local communities come and help us with the fish releases, with restoring the health of the river ecosystem. It’s really about bringing a community together around an environmentally important cause.

VO 15 At the Bushman’s Kloof farm dam, its time for Jeremy and his team to set the nets - this has been home to the rescued sandfish for the last four years, but in twenty four hours they will be returned to the wild.

VO 16 As the sun sets in the Cederberg, a crucial part of the rescue mission unfolds. Overnight the sandfish will swim into the nets, and soon they will make their final journey back to where they belong.

VO 17 When the next day dawns, there’s much anticipation - how many sandfish have they netted?

VO 18 It’s not long before they strike gold.

NATSOUND Cecilia: That’s fish. Govan: Ja, you never really know.

VO 19 Cecilia Cerrilla has been keeping a record of the numbers of sandfish rescued, raised and released. She recently completed her PHD on the sandfish at the University of Cape Town - painstakingly collecting data for months.

NATSOUND Cecilia: And now we need the lid. Govan: That’s a very scientific move there. Cecilia: Otherwise they jump.

VO 20 This is the nervewracking part of the mission - the sandfish are placed in buckets and then transported by road to the river. It takes over an hour. There can be fatalities.

VO 21 It’s a relief when the team finally arrives.

VO 22 Cecilia must first tag them before their release.

UPSOUND Cecilia Cerrilla / Conservation biologist: It’s more or less the size of a grain of rice. So we’ll anaethetise the fish, measure, tag and then put him in recovery bucket and then within a couple of minutes they’re righting themselves and swimming normally.

VO 23 The good news is the sandfish are big.

NATSOUND Jeremy: What do we have here a world record?

UPSOUND Cecilia Cerrilla / Conservation Biologist: Its really important to release big fish because the data shows the bigger they are when you release them the more of a chance you have of them returning. It’s a good indicator of survival and of coming back to spawn and actually contributing to the next generation.

NATSOUND Govan: This is a big champ. This is a beautiful fish. And these rivers would have been packed with them. That’s my biggest catch of the year.

LINK: And now the real test begins. Can they make it up the river and survive?

VO 24 An underwater antenna close to where the Beidouw flows into the Doring River will read the tags that are embedded in the fish. They’ll pass over it during their spawning migration and that’ll give an accurate indication of this release’s success.

UPSOUND Jeremy Shelton: What we’ve seen over the last three years is a three fold increase in the spawning migration of sandfish up into the Biedouw river. We’ve seen that 180 200 fish get up to about five six hundred fish. It’s still low numbers, its still early days, we’ve got a long way to go but it’s a great start.

VO 25 As the last fish are released, I’m offered the chance to do the honours too. It’s not as easy as it looks.

LINK: You know, after seeing everything that they’ve been through and knowing how endangered they were, this feels like an absolute privilege..That’s not the first fish I’ve lost.

VO 26 With hard work… and hope … the sandfish could return to their former glory.

VO 27 Sarah believes its just a matter of time before future generations experience the joys of a sandfish migration, as she once did.

UPSOUND Sarah Fransman Subtitles: I have a lot of hope that it will continue. It is nice to stand on a high place and look at how they move in the water.

Sarah Fransman, who grew up in a cottage on the banks of the Biedouw river, remembers how the sandfish would make a wave, “the whole school would stretch from one side to the other”. There are also paintings on cave walls in the area showing sandfish migrations on a mythic scale.
metadata.Summary: This story will follow the urgent efforts to rescue the species from collapse. Led by the Freshwater Research Centre, a diverse team of scientists and local residents is undertaking Africa’s largest freshwater fish rescue. Their goal is to relocate thousands of vulnerable juvenile sandfish from drying river pools – where they are vulnerable to invasive species – into cleared, alien-free farm dams where they have a fighting chance at survival. Now, rescued sandfish that have been reared to a safe size will be released back into the wild. This will happen in the first week of September. Each is tagged with a microchip to track whether these fish return to their birthplace to spawn –the first real test of whether the intervention is working. This is a story about the extraordinary efforts of ordinary people to restore what’s about to be lost. It’s about how we choose to respond in the face of vanishing biodiversity. The sandfish are a vital part of the Olifants-Doring River system’s ecosystem. Characters: Sarah Fransman / Has lived in area her whole life and remembers watching the sandfish migration as a child. Jeremy Shelton / Scientist from the Freshwater Research Centre Cecilia Cerilla / PHD student writing her thesis on this
